world.setting: Coconut Cove, South Florida - a flat strip-mall town of scrub lots, chain-link fence, pancake franchises and hot asphalt, with a middle school, a police cruiser and a construction trailer in it.
world.register: Sunlit suburban Florida realism with a satirical edge: cheap paneling, golden shovels, TV news vans. Everything is ordinary, daylight and slightly absurd - never mythic, never noir.

roy.name: Roy Eberhardt
roy.look: A slight twelve-year-old American boy with short sandy-brown hair, a plain t-shirt, jeans and sneakers, a backpack on one shoulder, alert and watchful.
roy.note: The new kid, just moved from Montana - the polite, careful one who finds the bureaucratic seam and wins the lot with a public question.

delinko.name: Officer David Delinko
delinko.look: A young uniformed patrol officer in a short-sleeved police shirt with a badge and belt, close-cropped hair, clipboard and flashlight in hand.
delinko.note: The patrol cop who genuinely wants the case and is comically outranked - the book's honest portrait of a decent institution.

muckle.name: Chuck Muckle
muckle.look: A sharply dressed corporate executive in his forties, dark suit and tie, slicked receding hair, phone in hand.
muckle.note: The Mother Paula's corporate VP - the same bully as Dana, in a suit, on a speakerphone from an air-conditioned office in Memphis.

curly.name: Curly
curly.look: A bald, heavyset middle-aged construction foreman, sweating through a short-sleeved work shirt, hard hat on, keys on his belt.
curly.note: The site foreman - not a villain, a man holding a shovel for somebody in another city, terrorized down a phone line.

fingers.name: Mullet Fingers
fingers.look: A wiry, sunburnt boy of about thirteen with tangled bleached-blond hair, no shoes, a torn t-shirt and mud-streaked shorts, always mid-run.
fingers.note: The barefoot runaway who sabotages the site - cares most, but exists on no paper, so he can never win the fight.

dana.name: Dana Matherson
dana.look: A big, heavy fourteen-year-old boy, sweating, buzz-cut hair, a stretched t-shirt and untied sneakers, thick hands.
dana.note: The school bully on the bus - the street-level version of the same force Mother Paula's applies from a corporate office.

beatrice.name: Beatrice Leep
beatrice.look: A tall, athletic teenage girl in a soccer jersey and shorts, dark hair pulled back, wire-rim glasses, arms folded.
beatrice.note: The tough stepsister of Mullet Fingers and his only cover - she decides what Roy is allowed to know.

kimberly.name: Kimberly Lou Dixon
kimberly.look: A middle-aged woman sweating in a heavy grey wig, calico apron and granny costume, forcing a smile for the cameras.
kimberly.note: The fading actress who plays the Mother Paula mascot - the PR schedule the whole groundbreaking is built around.

busWindow.look: A yellow school bus stopped on a flat Florida street, smudged window glass, palms and low strip-mall roofs behind it in flat morning light.

scrubLot.look: The vacant scrub lot at East Oriole and Woodbury: sandy dirt, weeds, survey stakes with pink ribbon, chain-link fence, portable toilets, three small owl burrows in the ground.

trailer.look: The sweltering construction trailer - cheap wood paneling, a window AC unit, a desk with a phone and a half-eaten tuna sandwich, blueprints curling at the edges.

broomCloset.look: A cramped bleach-smelling janitorial closet at Trace Middle School - mop bucket, metal shelving, one bare bulb.

corporateOffice.look: An air-conditioned corporate office far away in Memphis: glass, a clean desk, a speakerphone - cold and quiet against the Florida heat.

groundbreaking.look: The groundbreaking ceremony on the lot: a row of golden shovels catching the sun, a podium with a microphone, TV news cameras and a small crowd of kids with placards.

ward.look: A plain county hospital room with a curtain rail and a bed, a clipboard of admission paperwork at the foot of it.

objects.why: The environmental impact statement - the missing file. This is the book's real weapon and the climax turns on naming it out loud.
Ordinances, records requests, federal investigation - the procedural machinery that actually stops the bulldozer.
The speakerphone: how corporate pressure travels down the chain to the foreman without ever visiting the lot.
Hard hats, survey stakes, bulldozers, the shovel Curly holds for somebody else.
The bus, Trace Middle School, the broom closet - the bully plot's whole geography.
The cash bribe and the stock price - money is what finally makes the company fold.
TV news cameras at the groundbreaking; the public moment is the pressure point.
NEW ICON NEEDED - a small burrowing owl standing at the mouth of a hole in the dirt. The book's subject, and nothing in the library stands in for it.
NEW ICON NEEDED - a ceremonial golden shovel. The single image of the groundbreaking and of the foreman's place in the chain.
Montana against Florida - Roy learning to love an unheroic landscape instead of the wilderness he misses.
Beatrice's household and the mother who refuses to claim Mullet Fingers - why he has no standing.
The bureaucratic seam: the exact soft spot Roy aims at instead of the bulldozer.

spine.claim: The book opens on a barefoot boy running past a school bus and promises a wild-kid adventure it is about to quietly withdraw.
Every act of sabotage - the stakes, the alligators, the snakes - only buys a day; the machine replants and reschedules.
The bully on the bus and the VP on the speakerphone are one behavior at two scales, and the people in the middle are only holding the shovel.
The win arrives as a public records question on camera: disclosure plus embarrassment, not heroics, is what saves the lot.
Hoot is not about loving nature but about learning where power is soft - find the missing file, and you win the lot.
